title: Make a hero
description: Design a Hero blueprint once, then make a whole party of heroes from it.

tasks.title: A blueprint for things that belong together
tasks.body: class Hero: starts a blueprint. Its __init__(self, name) method runs whenever a hero is made with Hero("Nova"), and self.name = name stores the name on that hero. Every object made from the class has its own attributes.
tasks.detail: self is the object being made or used. Python passes it in for you, so Hero("Nova") has one argument while __init__ has two parameters. Read an attribute with a dot: nova.name. Forgetting self. makes a plain local name that vanishes when __init__ ends.

tasks.code:
class Hero:
    def __init__(self, name, health=10):
        self.name = name
        self.health = health

nova = Hero("Nova")
kai = Hero("Kai", 12)
kai.health = kai.health - 3
print(nova.name, nova.health)
print(kai.name, kai.health)
tasks.note: Each Hero() call makes a separate object. Nova uses the default health, Kai gets 12, and changing kai.health leaves Nova alone.

tasks.question: If __init__ said health = health instead of self.health = health, what would nova.health do?
tasks.why: Without self., health is only a local name inside __init__. The object never gets a health attribute, so asking for one is an AttributeError.

tasks.prompt: Predict, then run: take self. off the health line and read the error. Then give Hero a third attribute, level, that always starts at 1.

Make a Hero object for each hero in the party.

1. Ask how many heroes are in the party (always at least 1), then each hero's name and health, as a whole number.
2. Make a Hero for each, with a name, a health, and a level that always starts at 1, and keep them in a list.
3. Print one line per hero, in order, like Nova: 10 health, level 1.
4. On the last line, print the name of the hero with the most health; if heroes tie, the first of them.
tasks.starter: # Define class Hero, then build the party
hints: __init__ takes self, the name and the health, and stores each on self. The level isn't a parameter at all: it is always 1.
Make each hero with Hero(name, health) and append it to a list. Then loop over the list for the lines, and keep the healthiest hero so far, replacing it only when one has more.
With other names: class Pet: with def __init__(self, kind): and self.kind = kind inside, then pets.append(Pet("cat")).

error_hints.text: An attribute is missing. Inside __init__, store each value with self., such as self.health = health.
Check that __init__ has self first, then the name and the health, and that Hero() is called with two values.
Inside __init__, use the parameter names from its def line. Outside it, read attributes through an object, like hero.name.
With Nova at 10 and Kai at 12, the lines are Nova: 10 health, level 1, then Kai: 12 health, level 1, and Kai.
A party of one: that hero is also the healthiest.
When heroes tie for the most health, the first of them is named: replace the best only when a hero has more.
Check heroes with no health left at all.

similar_example.note: A small class with one attribute from its argument and one that always starts the same. Your heroes also get compared.

other_ways.note: A method, line(), describes a hero. max() with a key finds the healthiest, and keeps the first when heroes tie. Next lesson is all about methods.
__str__ decides what print() shows for a hero. The highest health is found first, then the first hero who has it.
